8	
9	
10	## Introduction
11	
12	This document describes techniques for writing compiler backends that convert
13	the LLVM Intermediate Representation (IR) to code for a specified machine or
14	other languages.  Code intended for a specific machine can take the form of
15	either assembly code or binary code (usable for a JIT compiler).
16	
17	The backend of LLVM features a target-independent code generator that may
18	create output for several types of target CPUs --- including X86, PowerPC,
19	ARM, and SPARC.  The backend may also be used to generate code targeted at SPUs
20	of the Cell processor or GPUs to support the execution of compute kernels.
21	
22	The document focuses on existing examples found in subdirectories of
23	`llvm/lib/Target` in a downloaded LLVM release.  In particular, this document
24	focuses on the example of creating a static compiler (one that emits text
25	assembly) for a SPARC target, because SPARC has fairly standard
26	characteristics, such as a RISC instruction set and straightforward calling
27	conventions.
28	
29	### Audience
30	
31	The audience for this document is anyone who needs to write an LLVM backend to
32	generate code for a specific hardware or software target.
33	
34	### Prerequisite Reading
35	
36	These essential documents must be read before reading this document:
37	
38	* {doc}`LLVM Language Reference Manual <LangRef>` --- a reference manual for
39	  the LLVM assembly language.
40	
41	* {doc}`CodeGenerator` --- a guide to the components (classes and code
42	  generation algorithms) for translating the LLVM internal representation into
43	  machine code for a specified target.  Pay particular attention to the
44	  descriptions of code generation stages: Instruction Selection, Scheduling and
45	  Formation, SSA-based Optimization, Register Allocation, Prolog/Epilog Code
46	  Insertion, Late Machine Code Optimizations, and Code Emission.
47	
48	* {doc}`TableGen/index` --- a document that describes the TableGen
49	  (`tblgen`) application that manages domain-specific information to support
50	  LLVM code generation.  TableGen processes input from a target description
51	  file (`.td` suffix) and generates C++ code that can be used for code
52	  generation.
53	
54	* {doc}`WritingAnLLVMPass` --- The assembly printer is a `FunctionPass`, as
55	  are several `SelectionDAG` processing steps.
56	
57	To follow the SPARC examples in this document, have a copy of [The SPARC
58	Architecture Manual, Version 8] for
59	reference.  For details about the ARM instruction set, refer to the [ARM
60	Architecture Reference Manual].  For more about
61	the GNU Assembler format (`GAS`), see [Using As], especially for the
62	assembly printer.  "Using As" contains a list of target machine dependent
63	features.
64	
65	[The SPARC Architecture Manual, Version 8]: http://www.sparc.org/standards/V8.pdf
66	[ARM Architecture Reference Manual]: http://infocenter.arm.com/
67	[Using As]: http://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/as/index.html
68	
69	### Basic Steps
70	
71	To write a compiler backend for LLVM that converts the LLVM IR to code for a
72	specified target (machine or other language), follow these steps:
73	
74	* Create a subclass of the `TargetMachine` class that describes
75	  characteristics of your target machine.  Copy existing examples of specific
76	  `TargetMachine` class and header files; for example, start with
77	  `SparcTargetMachine.cpp` and `SparcTargetMachine.h`, but change the file
78	  names for your target.  Similarly, change code that references "`Sparc`" to
79	  reference your target.
80	
81	* Describe the register set of the target.  Use TableGen to generate code for
82	  register definition, register aliases, and register classes from a
83	  target-specific `RegisterInfo.td` input file.  You should also write
84	  additional code for a subclass of the `TargetRegisterInfo` class that
85	  represents the class register file data used for register allocation and also
86	  describes the interactions between registers.
87	
88	* Describe the instruction set of the target.  Use TableGen to generate code
89	  for target-specific instructions from target-specific versions of
90	  `TargetInstrFormats.td` and `TargetInstrInfo.td`.  You should write
91	  additional code for a subclass of the `TargetInstrInfo` class to represent
92	  machine instructions supported by the target machine.
93	
94	* Describe the selection and conversion of the LLVM IR from a Directed Acyclic
95	  Graph (DAG) representation of instructions to native target-specific
96	  instructions.  Use TableGen to generate code that matches patterns and
97	  selects instructions based on additional information in a target-specific
98	  version of `TargetInstrInfo.td`.  Write code for `XXXISelDAGToDAG.cpp`,
99	  where `XXX` identifies the specific target, to perform pattern matching and
100	  DAG-to-DAG instruction selection.  Also write code in `XXXISelLowering.cpp`
101	  to replace or remove operations and data types that are not supported
102	  natively in a SelectionDAG.
103	
104	* Write code for an assembly printer that converts LLVM IR to a GAS format for
105	  your target machine.  You should add assembly strings to the instructions
106	  defined in your target-specific version of `TargetInstrInfo.td`.  You
107	  should also write code for a subclass of `AsmPrinter` that performs the
108	  LLVM-to-assembly conversion and a trivial subclass of `TargetAsmInfo`.
109	
110	* Optionally, add support for subtargets (i.e., variants with different
111	  capabilities).  You should also write code for a subclass of the
112	  `TargetSubtarget` class, which allows you to use the `-mcpu=` and
113	  `-mattr=` command-line options.
114	
115	* Optionally, add JIT support and create a machine code emitter (subclass of
116	  `TargetJITInfo`) that is used to emit binary code directly into memory.
117	
118	In the `.cpp` and `.h`. files, initially stub up these methods and then
119	implement them later.  Initially, you may not know which private members that
120	the class will need and which components will need to be subclassed.
121	
122	### Preliminaries
123	
124	To actually create your compiler backend, you need to create and modify a few
125	files.  The absolute minimum is discussed here.  But to actually use the LLVM
126	target-independent code generator, you must perform the steps described in the
127	{doc}`LLVM Target-Independent Code Generator <CodeGenerator>` document.
128	
129	First, you should create a subdirectory under `lib/Target` to hold all the
130	files related to your target.  If your target is called "Dummy", create the
131	directory `lib/Target/Dummy`.
132	
133	In this new directory, create a `CMakeLists.txt`.  It is easiest to copy a
134	`CMakeLists.txt` of another target and modify it.  It should at least contain
135	the `LLVM_TARGET_DEFINITIONS` variable. The library can be named `LLVMDummy`
136	(for example, see the MIPS target).  Alternatively, you can split the library
137	into `LLVMDummyCodeGen` and `LLVMDummyAsmPrinter`, the latter of which
138	should be implemented in a subdirectory below `lib/Target/Dummy` (for example,
139	see the PowerPC target).
140	
141	Note that these two naming schemes are hardcoded into `llvm-config`.  Using
142	any other naming scheme will confuse `llvm-config` and produce a lot of
143	(seemingly unrelated) linker errors when linking `llc`.
144	
145	To make your target actually do something, you need to implement a subclass of
146	`TargetMachine`.  This implementation should typically be in the file
147	`lib/Target/DummyTargetMachine.cpp`, but any file in the `lib/Target`
148	directory will be built and should work.  To use LLVM's target-independent code
149	generator, you should do what all current machine backends do: create a
150	subclass of `CodeGenTargetMachineImpl`.  (To create a target from scratch, create a
151	subclass of `TargetMachine`.)
152	
153	To get LLVM to actually build and link your target, you need to run `cmake`
154	with `-DLLVM_EXPERIMENTAL_TARGETS_TO_BUILD=Dummy`. This will build your
155	target without needing to add it to the list of all the targets.
156	
157	Once your target is stable, you can add it to the `LLVM_ALL_TARGETS` variable
158	located in the main `CMakeLists.txt`.
159	
160	## Target Machine
161	
162	`CodeGenTargetMachineImpl` is designed as a base class for targets implemented with
163	the LLVM target-independent code generator. The `CodeGenTargetMachineImpl` class
164	should be specialized by a concrete target class that implements the various
165	virtual methods.  `CodeGenTargetMachineImpl` is defined as a subclass of
166	`TargetMachine` in `include/llvm/CodeGen/CodeGenTargetMachineImpl.h`.  The
167	`TargetMachine` class implementation (`include/llvm/Target/TargetMachine.cpp`)
168	also processes numerous command-line options.
169	
170	To create a concrete target-specific subclass of `CodeGenTargetMachineImpl`, start
171	by copying an existing `TargetMachine` class and header.  You should name the
172	files that you create to reflect your specific target.  For instance, for the
173	SPARC target, name the files `SparcTargetMachine.h` and
174	`SparcTargetMachine.cpp`.
175	
176	For a target machine `XXX`, the implementation of `XXXTargetMachine` must
177	have access methods to obtain objects that represent target components.  These
178	methods are named `get*Info`, and are intended to obtain the instruction set
179	(`getInstrInfo`), register set (`getRegisterInfo`), stack frame layout
180	(`getFrameInfo`), and similar information.  `XXXTargetMachine` must also
181	implement the `getDataLayout` method to access an object with target-specific
182	data characteristics, such as data type size and alignment requirements.
183	
184	For instance, for the SPARC target, the header file `SparcTargetMachine.h`
185	declares prototypes for several `get*Info` and `getDataLayout` methods that
186	simply return a class member.
187	
188	```c++
189	namespace llvm {
190	
191	class Module;
192	
193	class SparcTargetMachine : public CodeGenTargetMachineImpl {
194	  const DataLayout DataLayout;       // Calculates type size & alignment
195	  SparcSubtarget Subtarget;
196	  SparcInstrInfo InstrInfo;
197	  TargetFrameInfo FrameInfo;
198	
199	protected:
200	  virtual const TargetAsmInfo *createTargetAsmInfo() const;
201	
202	public:
203	  SparcTargetMachine(const Module &M, const std::string &FS);
204	
205	  virtual const SparcInstrInfo *getInstrInfo() const {return &InstrInfo; }
206	  virtual const TargetFrameInfo *getFrameInfo() const {return &FrameInfo; }
207	  virtual const TargetSubtarget *getSubtargetImpl() const{return &Subtarget; }
208	  virtual const TargetRegisterInfo *getRegisterInfo() const {
209	    return &InstrInfo.getRegisterInfo();
210	  }
211	  virtual const DataLayout *getDataLayout() const { return &DataLayout; }
212	
213	  // Pass Pipeline Configuration
214	  virtual bool addInstSelector(PassManagerBase &PM, bool Fast);
215	  virtual bool addPreEmitPass(PassManagerBase &PM, bool Fast);
216	};
217	
218	} // end namespace llvm
219	```
220	
221	* `getInstrInfo()`
222	* `getRegisterInfo()`
223	* `getFrameInfo()`
224	* `getDataLayout()`
225	* `getSubtargetImpl()`
226	
227	For some targets, you also need to support the following methods:
228	
229	* `getTargetLowering()`
230	* `getJITInfo()`
231	
232	Some architectures, such as GPUs, do not support jumping to an arbitrary
233	program location and implement branching using masked execution and loop using
234	special instructions around the loop body. In order to avoid CFG modifications
235	that introduce irreducible control flow not handled by such hardware, a target
236	must call `setRequiresStructuredCFG(true)` when being initialized.
237	
238	In addition, the `XXXTargetMachine` constructor should specify a
239	`TargetDescription` string that determines the data layout for the target
240	machine, including characteristics such as pointer size, alignment, and
241	endianness.  For example, the constructor for `SparcTargetMachine` contains
242	the following:
243	
244	```c++
245	SparcTargetMachine::SparcTargetMachine(const Module &M, const std::string &FS)
246	  : DataLayout("E-p:32:32-f128:128:128"),
247	    Subtarget(M, FS), InstrInfo(Subtarget),
248	    FrameInfo(TargetFrameInfo::StackGrowsDown, 8, 0) {
249	}
250	```
251	
252	Hyphens separate portions of the `TargetDescription` string.
253	
254	* An upper-case "`E`" in the string indicates a big-endian target data model.
255	  A lower-case "`e`" indicates little-endian.
256	
257	* "`p:`" is followed by pointer information: size, ABI alignment, and
258	  preferred alignment.  If only two figures follow "`p:`", then the first
259	  value is pointer size, and the second value is both ABI and preferred
260	  alignment.
261	
262	* Then a letter for numeric type alignment: "`i`", "`f`", "`v`", or
263	  "`a`" (corresponding to integer, floating point, vector, or aggregate).
264	  "`i`", "`v`", or "`a`" are followed by ABI alignment and preferred
265	  alignment. "`f`" is followed by three values: the first indicates the size
266	  of a long double, then ABI alignment, and then ABI preferred alignment.
267	
268	## Target Registration
269	
270	You must also register your target with the `TargetRegistry`, which is what
271	other LLVM tools use to be able to lookup and use your target at runtime.  The
272	`TargetRegistry` can be used directly, but for most targets there are helper
273	templates which should take care of the work for you.
274	
275	All targets should declare a global `Target` object which is used to
276	represent the target during registration.  Then, in the target's `TargetInfo`
277	library, the target should define that object and use the `RegisterTarget`
278	template to register the target.  For example, the Sparc registration code
279	looks like this:
280	
281	```c++
282	Target llvm::getTheSparcTarget();
283	
284	extern "C" void LLVMInitializeSparcTargetInfo() {
285	  RegisterTarget<Triple::sparc, /*HasJIT=*/false>
286	    X(getTheSparcTarget(), "sparc", "Sparc");
287	}
288	```
289	
290	This allows the `TargetRegistry` to look up the target by name or by target
291	triple.  In addition, most targets will also register additional features which
292	are available in separate libraries.  These registration steps are separate,
293	because some clients may wish to only link in some parts of the target --- the
294	JIT code generator does not require the use of the assembler printer, for
295	example.  Here is an example of registering the Sparc assembly printer:
296	
297	```c++
298	extern "C" void LLVMInitializeSparcAsmPrinter() {
299	  RegisterAsmPrinter<SparcAsmPrinter> X(getTheSparcTarget());
300	}
301	```
302	
303	For more information, see "[`llvm/Target/TargetRegistry.h`][TargetRegistry]".
304	
305	[TargetRegistry]: doxygen:TargetRegistry_8h-source.html
306	
307	## Register Set and Register Classes
308	
309	You should describe a concrete target-specific class that represents the
310	register file of a target machine.  This class is called `XXXRegisterInfo`
311	(where `XXX` identifies the target) and represents the class register file
312	data that is used for register allocation.  It also describes the interactions
313	between registers.
314	
315	You also need to define register classes to categorize related registers.  A
316	register class should be added for groups of registers that are all treated the
317	same way for some instruction.  Typical examples are register classes for
318	integer, floating-point, or vector registers.  A register allocator allows an
319	instruction to use any register in a specified register class to perform the
320	instruction in a similar manner.  Register classes allocate virtual registers
321	to instructions from these sets, and register classes let the
322	target-independent register allocator automatically choose the actual
323	registers.
324	
325	Much of the code for registers, including register definition, register
326	aliases, and register classes, is generated by TableGen from
327	`XXXRegisterInfo.td` input files and placed in `XXXGenRegisterInfo.h.inc`
328	and `XXXGenRegisterInfo.inc` output files.  Some of the code in the
329	implementation of `XXXRegisterInfo` requires hand-coding.
330	
331	### Defining a Register
332	
333	The `XXXRegisterInfo.td` file typically starts with register definitions for
334	a target machine.  The `Register` class (specified in `Target.td`) is used
335	to define an object for each register.  The specified string `n` becomes the
336	`Name` of the register.  The basic `Register` object does not have any
337	subregisters and does not specify any aliases.
338	
339	```text
340	class Register<string n> {
341	  string Namespace = "";
342	  string AsmName = n;
343	  string Name = n;
344	  int SpillSize = 0;
345	  int SpillAlignment = 0;
346	  list<Register> Aliases = [];
347	  list<Register> SubRegs = [];
348	  list<int> DwarfNumbers = [];
349	}
350	```
351	
352	For example, in the `X86RegisterInfo.td` file, there are register definitions
353	that utilize the `Register` class, such as:
354	
355	```text
356	def AL : Register<"AL">, DwarfRegNum<[0, 0, 0]>;
357	```
358	
359	This defines the register `AL` and assigns it values (with `DwarfRegNum`)
360	that are used by `gcc`, `gdb`, or a debug information writer to identify a
361	register.  For register `AL`, `DwarfRegNum` takes an array of 3 values
362	representing 3 different modes: the first element is for X86-64, the second for
363	exception handling (EH) on X86-32, and the third is generic. -1 is a special
364	Dwarf number that indicates the gcc number is undefined, and -2 indicates the
365	register number is invalid for this mode.
366	
367	From the previously described line in the `X86RegisterInfo.td` file, TableGen
368	generates this code in the `X86GenRegisterInfo.inc` file:
369	
370	```c++
371	static const unsigned GR8[] = { X86::AL, ... };
372	
373	const unsigned AL_AliasSet[] = { X86::AX, X86::EAX, X86::RAX, 0 };
374	
375	const TargetRegisterDesc RegisterDescriptors[] = {
376	  ...
377	{ "AL", "AL", AL_AliasSet, Empty_SubRegsSet, Empty_SubRegsSet, AL_SuperRegsSet }, ...
378	```
379	
380	From the register info file, TableGen generates a `TargetRegisterDesc` object
381	for each register.  `TargetRegisterDesc` is defined in
382	`include/llvm/Target/TargetRegisterInfo.h` with the following fields:
383	
384	```c++
385	struct TargetRegisterDesc {
386	  const char     *AsmName;      // Assembly language name for the register
387	  const char     *Name;         // Printable name for the reg (for debugging)
388	  const unsigned *AliasSet;     // Register Alias Set
389	  const unsigned *SubRegs;      // Sub-register set
390	  const unsigned *ImmSubRegs;   // Immediate sub-register set
391	  const unsigned *SuperRegs;    // Super-register set
392	};
393	```
394	
395	TableGen uses the entire target description file (`.td`) to determine text
396	names for the register (in the `AsmName` and `Name` fields of
397	`TargetRegisterDesc`) and the relationships of other registers to the defined
398	register (in the other `TargetRegisterDesc` fields).  In this example, other
399	definitions establish the registers "`AX`", "`EAX`", and "`RAX`" as
400	aliases for one another, so TableGen generates a null-terminated array
401	(`AL_AliasSet`) for this register alias set.
402	
403	The `Register` class is commonly used as a base class for more complex
404	classes.  In `Target.td`, the `Register` class is the base for the
405	`RegisterWithSubRegs` class that is used to define registers that need to
406	specify subregisters in the `SubRegs` list, as shown here:
407	
408	```text
409	class RegisterWithSubRegs<string n, list<Register> subregs> : Register<n> {
410	  let SubRegs = subregs;
411	}
412	```
413	
414	In `SparcRegisterInfo.td`, additional register classes are defined for SPARC:
415	a `Register` subclass, `SparcReg`, and further subclasses: `Ri`, `Rf`,
416	and `Rd`.  SPARC registers are identified by 5-bit ID numbers, which is a
417	feature common to these subclasses.  Note the use of "`let`" expressions to
418	override values that are initially defined in a superclass (such as `SubRegs`
419	field in the `Rd` class).
420	
421	```text
422	class SparcReg<string n> : Register<n> {
423	  field bits<5> Num;
424	  let Namespace = "SP";
425	}
426	// Ri - 32-bit integer registers
427	class Ri<bits<5> num, string n> :
428	SparcReg<n> {
429	  let Num = num;
430	}
431	// Rf - 32-bit floating-point registers
432	class Rf<bits<5> num, string n> :
433	SparcReg<n> {
434	  let Num = num;
435	}
436	// Rd - Slots in the FP register file for 64-bit floating-point values.
437	class Rd<bits<5> num, string n, list<Register> subregs> : SparcReg<n> {
438	  let Num = num;
439	  let SubRegs = subregs;
440	}
441	```
442	
443	In the `SparcRegisterInfo.td` file, there are register definitions that
444	utilize these subclasses of `Register`, such as:
445	
446	```text
447	def G0 : Ri< 0, "G0">, DwarfRegNum<[0]>;
448	def G1 : Ri< 1, "G1">, DwarfRegNum<[1]>;
449	...
450	def F0 : Rf< 0, "F0">, DwarfRegNum<[32]>;
451	def F1 : Rf< 1, "F1">, DwarfRegNum<[33]>;
452	...
453	def D0 : Rd< 0, "F0", [F0, F1]>, DwarfRegNum<[32]>;
454	def D1 : Rd< 2, "F2", [F2, F3]>, DwarfRegNum<[34]>;
455	```
456	
457	The last two registers shown above (`D0` and `D1`) are double-precision
458	floating-point registers that are aliases for pairs of single-precision
459	floating-point sub-registers.  In addition to aliases, the sub-register and
460	super-register relationships of the defined register are in fields of a
461	register's `TargetRegisterDesc`.
462	
463	### Defining a Register Class
464	
465	The `RegisterClass` class (specified in `Target.td`) is used to define an
466	object that represents a group of related registers and also defines the
467	default allocation order of the registers.  A target description file
468	`XXXRegisterInfo.td` that uses `Target.td` can construct register classes
469	using the following class:
470	
471	```text
472	class RegisterClass<string namespace,
473	list<ValueType> regTypes, int alignment, dag regList> {
474	  string Namespace = namespace;
475	  list<ValueType> RegTypes = regTypes;
476	  int Size = 0;  // spill size, in bits; zero lets tblgen pick the size
477	  int Alignment = alignment;
478	
479	  // CopyCost is the cost of copying a value between two registers
480	  // default value 1 means a single instruction
481	  // A negative value means copying is extremely expensive or impossible
482	  int CopyCost = 1;
483	  dag MemberList = regList;
484	
485	  // for register classes that are subregisters of this class
486	  list<RegisterClass> SubRegClassList = [];
487	
488	  code MethodProtos = [{}];  // to insert arbitrary code
489	  code MethodBodies = [{}];
490	}
491	```
492	
493	To define a `RegisterClass`, use the following 4 arguments:
494	
495	* The first argument of the definition is the name of the namespace.
496	
497	* The second argument is a list of `ValueType` register type values that are
498	  defined in `include/llvm/CodeGen/ValueTypes.td`.  Defined values include
499	  integer types (such as `i16`, `i32`, and `i1` for Boolean),
500	  floating-point types (`f32`, `f64`), and vector types (for example,
501	  `v8i16` for an `8 x i16` vector).  All registers in a `RegisterClass`
502	  must have the same `ValueType`, but some registers may store vector data in
503	  different configurations.  For example a register that can process a 128-bit
504	  vector may be able to handle 16 8-bit integer elements, 8 16-bit integers, 4
505	  32-bit integers, and so on.
506	
507	* The third argument of the `RegisterClass` definition specifies the
508	  alignment required of the registers when they are stored or loaded to
509	  memory.
510	
511	* The final argument, `regList`, specifies which registers are in this class.
512	  If an alternative allocation order method is not specified, then `regList`
513	  also defines the order of allocation used by the register allocator.  Besides
514	  simply listing registers with `(add R0, R1, ...)`, more advanced set
515	  operators are available.  See `include/llvm/Target/Target.td` for more
516	  information.
517	
518	In `SparcRegisterInfo.td`, three `RegisterClass` objects are defined:
519	`FPRegs`, `DFPRegs`, and `IntRegs`.  For all three register classes, the
520	first argument defines the namespace with the string "`SP`".  `FPRegs`
521	defines a group of 32 single-precision floating-point registers (`F0` to
522	`F31`); `DFPRegs` defines a group of 16 double-precision registers
523	(`D0-D15`).
524	
525	```text
526	// F0, F1, F2, ..., F31
527	def FPRegs : RegisterClass<"SP", [f32], 32, (sequence "F%u", 0, 31)>;
528	
529	def DFPRegs : RegisterClass<"SP", [f64], 64,
530	                            (add D0, D1, D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D7, D8,
531	                                 D9, D10, D11, D12, D13, D14, D15)>;
532	
533	def IntRegs : RegisterClass<"SP", [i32], 32,
534	    (add L0, L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6, L7,
535	         I0, I1, I2, I3, I4, I5,
536	         O0, O1, O2, O3, O4, O5, O7,
537	         G1,
538	         // Non-allocatable regs:
539	         G2, G3, G4,
540	         O6,        // stack ptr
541	         I6,        // frame ptr
542	         I7,        // return address
543	         G0,        // constant zero
544	         G5, G6, G7 // reserved for kernel
545	    )>;
546	```
547	
548	Using `SparcRegisterInfo.td` with TableGen generates several output files
549	that are intended for inclusion in other source code that you write.
550	`SparcRegisterInfo.td` generates `SparcGenRegisterInfo.h.inc`, which should
551	be included in the header file for the implementation of the SPARC register
552	implementation that you write (`SparcRegisterInfo.h`).  In
553	`SparcGenRegisterInfo.h.inc` a new structure is defined called
554	`SparcGenRegisterInfo` that uses `TargetRegisterInfo` as its base.  It also
555	specifies types, based upon the defined register classes: `DFPRegsClass`,
556	`FPRegsClass`, and `IntRegsClass`.
557	
558	`SparcRegisterInfo.td` also generates `SparcGenRegisterInfo.inc`, which is
559	included at the bottom of `SparcRegisterInfo.cpp`, the SPARC register
560	implementation.  The code below shows only the generated integer registers and
561	associated register classes.  The order of registers in `IntRegs` reflects
562	the order in the definition of `IntRegs` in the target description file.
563	
564	```c++
565	// IntRegs Register Class...
566	static const unsigned IntRegs[] = {
567	  SP::L0, SP::L1, SP::L2, SP::L3, SP::L4, SP::L5,
568	  SP::L6, SP::L7, SP::I0, SP::I1, SP::I2, SP::I3,
569	  SP::I4, SP::I5, SP::O0, SP::O1, SP::O2, SP::O3,
570	  SP::O4, SP::O5, SP::O7, SP::G1, SP::G2, SP::G3,
571	  SP::G4, SP::O6, SP::I6, SP::I7, SP::G0, SP::G5,
572	  SP::G6, SP::G7,
573	};
574	
575	// IntRegsVTs Register Class Value Types...
576	static const MVT::ValueType IntRegsVTs[] = {
577	  MVT::i32, MVT::Other
578	};
579	
580	namespace SP {   // Register class instances
581	  DFPRegsClass    DFPRegsRegClass;
582	  FPRegsClass     FPRegsRegClass;
583	  IntRegsClass    IntRegsRegClass;
584	...
585	  // IntRegs Sub-register Classes...
586	  static const TargetRegisterClass* const IntRegsSubRegClasses [] = {
587	    NULL
588	  };
589	...
590	  // IntRegs Super-register Classes..
591	  static const TargetRegisterClass* const IntRegsSuperRegClasses [] = {
592	    NULL
593	  };
594	...
595	  // IntRegs Register Class sub-classes...
596	  static const TargetRegisterClass* const IntRegsSubclasses [] = {
597	    NULL
598	  };
599	...
600	  // IntRegs Register Class super-classes...
601	  static const TargetRegisterClass* const IntRegsSuperclasses [] = {
602	    NULL
603	  };
604	
605	  IntRegsClass::IntRegsClass() : TargetRegisterClass(IntRegsRegClassID,
606	    IntRegsVTs, IntRegsSubclasses, IntRegsSuperclasses, IntRegsSubRegClasses,
607	    IntRegsSuperRegClasses, 4, 4, 1, IntRegs, IntRegs + 32) {}
608	}
609	```
610	
611	The register allocators will avoid using reserved registers, and callee saved
612	registers are not used until all the volatile registers have been used.  That
613	is usually good enough, but in some cases it may be necessary to provide custom
614	allocation orders.
615	
616	### Implement a subclass of `TargetRegisterInfo`
617	
618	The final step is to hand code portions of `XXXRegisterInfo`, which
619	implements the interface described in `TargetRegisterInfo.h` (see
620	{ref}`TargetRegisterInfo`).  These functions return `0`, `NULL`, or
621	`false`, unless overridden.  Here is a list of functions that are overridden
622	for the SPARC implementation in `SparcRegisterInfo.cpp`:
623	
624	* `getCalleeSavedRegs` --- Returns a list of callee-saved registers in the
625	  order of the desired callee-save stack frame offset.
626	
627	* `getReservedRegs` --- Returns a bitset indexed by physical register
628	  numbers, indicating if a particular register is unavailable.
629	
630	* `hasFP` --- Return a Boolean indicating if a function should have a
631	  dedicated frame pointer register.
632	
633	* `eliminateCallFramePseudoInstr` --- If call frame setup or destroy pseudo
634	  instructions are used, this can be called to eliminate them.
635	
636	* `eliminateFrameIndex` --- Eliminate abstract frame indices from
637	  instructions that may use them.
638	
639	* `emitPrologue` --- Insert prologue code into the function.
640	
641	* `emitEpilogue` --- Insert epilogue code into the function.
642	
643	(instruction-set)=
644	
645	## Instruction Set
646	
647	During the early stages of code generation, the LLVM IR code is converted to a
648	`SelectionDAG` with nodes that are instances of the `SDNode` class
649	containing target instructions.  An `SDNode` has an opcode, operands, type
650	requirements, and operation properties.  For example, is an operation
651	commutative, does an operation load from memory.  The various operation node
652	types are described in the `include/llvm/CodeGen/SelectionDAGNodes.h` file
653	(values of the `NodeType` enum in the `ISD` namespace).
654	
655	TableGen uses the following target description (`.td`) input files to
656	generate much of the code for instruction definition:
657	
658	* `Target.td` --- Where the `Instruction`, `Operand`, `InstrInfo`, and
659	  other fundamental classes are defined.
660	
661	* `TargetSelectionDAG.td` --- Used by `SelectionDAG` instruction selection
662	  generators, contains `SDTC*` classes (selection DAG type constraint),
663	  definitions of `SelectionDAG` nodes (such as `imm`, `cond`, `bb`,
664	  `add`, `fadd`, `sub`), and pattern support (`Pattern`, `Pat`,
665	  `PatFrag`, `PatLeaf`, `ComplexPattern`.
666	
667	* `XXXInstrFormats.td` --- Patterns for definitions of target-specific
668	  instructions.
669	
670	* `XXXInstrInfo.td` --- Target-specific definitions of instruction templates,
671	  condition codes, and instructions of an instruction set.  For architecture
672	  modifications, a different file name may be used.  For example, for Pentium
673	  with SSE instruction, this file is `X86InstrSSE.td`, and for Pentium with
674	  MMX, this file is `X86InstrMMX.td`.
675	
676	There is also a target-specific `XXX.td` file, where `XXX` is the name of
677	the target.  The `XXX.td` file includes the other `.td` input files, but
678	its contents are only directly important for subtargets.
679	
680	You should describe a concrete target-specific class `XXXInstrInfo` that
681	represents machine instructions supported by a target machine.
682	`XXXInstrInfo` contains an array of `XXXInstrDescriptor` objects, each of
683	which describes one instruction.  An instruction descriptor defines:
684	
685	* Opcode mnemonic
686	* Number of operands
687	* List of implicit register definitions and uses
688	* Target-independent properties (such as memory access, is commutable)
689	* Target-specific flags
690	
691	The Instruction class (defined in `Target.td`) is mostly used as a base for
692	more complex instruction classes.
693	
694	```text
695	class Instruction {
696	  string Namespace = "";
697	  dag OutOperandList;    // A dag containing the MI def operand list.
698	  dag InOperandList;     // A dag containing the MI use operand list.
699	  string AsmString = ""; // The .s format to print the instruction with.
700	  list<dag> Pattern;     // Set to the DAG pattern for this instruction.
701	  list<Register> Uses = [];
702	  list<Register> Defs = [];
703	  list<Predicate> Predicates = [];  // predicates turned into isel match code
704	  ... remainder not shown for space ...
705	}
706	```
707	
708	A `SelectionDAG` node (`SDNode`) should contain an object representing a
709	target-specific instruction that is defined in `XXXInstrInfo.td`.  The
710	instruction objects should represent instructions from the architecture manual
711	of the target machine (such as the SPARC Architecture Manual for the SPARC
712	target).
713	
714	A single instruction from the architecture manual is often modeled as multiple
715	target instructions, depending upon its operands.  For example, a manual might
716	describe an add instruction that takes a register or an immediate operand.  An
717	LLVM target could model this with two instructions named `ADDri` and
718	`ADDrr`.
719	
720	You should define a class for each instruction category and define each opcode
721	as a subclass of the category with appropriate parameters such as the fixed
722	binary encoding of opcodes and extended opcodes.  You should map the register
723	bits to the bits of the instruction in which they are encoded (for the JIT).
724	Also you should specify how the instruction should be printed when the
725	automatic assembly printer is used.
726	
727	As is described in the SPARC Architecture Manual, Version 8, there are three
728	major 32-bit formats for instructions.  Format 1 is only for the `CALL`
729	instruction.  Format 2 is for branch on condition codes and `SETHI` (set high
730	bits of a register) instructions.  Format 3 is for other instructions.
731	
732	Each of these formats has corresponding classes in `SparcInstrFormat.td`.
733	`InstSP` is a base class for other instruction classes.  Additional base
734	classes are specified for more precise formats: for example in
735	`SparcInstrFormat.td`, `F2_1` is for `SETHI`, and `F2_2` is for
736	branches.  There are three other base classes: `F3_1` for register/register
737	operations, `F3_2` for register/immediate operations, and `F3_3` for
738	floating-point operations.  `SparcInstrInfo.td` also adds the base class
739	`Pseudo` for synthetic SPARC instructions.
740	
741	`SparcInstrInfo.td` largely consists of operand and instruction definitions
742	for the SPARC target.  In `SparcInstrInfo.td`, the following target
743	description file entry, `LDrr`, defines the Load Integer instruction for a
744	Word (the `LD` SPARC opcode) from a memory address to a register.  The first
745	parameter, the value 3 (`11`{sub}`2`), is the operation value for this
746	category of operation.  The second parameter (`000000`{sub}`2`) is the
747	specific operation value for `LD`/Load Word.  The third parameter is the
748	output destination, which is a register operand and defined in the `Register`
749	target description file (`IntRegs`).
750	
751	```text
752	def LDrr : F3_1 <3, 0b000000, (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins (MEMrr $rs1, $rs2):$addr),
753	                 "ld [$addr], $dst",
754	                 [(set i32:$dst, (load ADDRrr:$addr))]>;
755	```
756	
757	The fourth parameter is the input source, which uses the address operand
758	`MEMrr` that is defined earlier in `SparcInstrInfo.td`:
759	
760	```text
761	def MEMrr : Operand<i32> {
762	  let PrintMethod = "printMemOperand";
763	  let MIOperandInfo = (ops IntRegs, IntRegs);
764	}
765	```
766	
767	The fifth parameter is a string that is used by the assembly printer and can be
768	left as an empty string until the assembly printer interface is implemented.
769	The sixth and final parameter is the pattern used to match the instruction
770	during the SelectionDAG Select Phase described in {doc}`CodeGenerator`.
771	This parameter is detailed in the next section, {ref}`instruction-selector`.
772	
773	Instruction class definitions are not overloaded for different operand types,
774	so separate versions of instructions are needed for register, memory, or
775	immediate value operands.  For example, to perform a Load Integer instruction
776	for a Word from an immediate operand to a register, the following instruction
777	class is defined:
778	
779	```text
780	def LDri : F3_2 <3, 0b000000, (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins (MEMri $rs1, $simm13):$addr),
781	                 "ld [$addr], $dst",
782	                 [(set i32:$rd, (load ADDRri:$addr))]>;
783	```
784	
785	Writing these definitions for so many similar instructions can involve a lot of
786	cut and paste.  In `.td` files, the `multiclass` directive enables the
787	creation of templates to define several instruction classes at once (using the
788	`defm` directive).  For example in `SparcInstrInfo.td`, the `multiclass`
789	pattern `F3_12` is defined to create 2 instruction classes each time
790	`F3_12` is invoked:
791	
792	```text
793	multiclass F3_12 <string OpcStr, bits<6> Op3Val, SDNode OpNode> {
794	  def rr  : F3_1 <2, Op3Val,
795	                 (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins IntRegs:$rs1, IntRegs:$rs1),
796	                 !strconcat(OpcStr, " $rs1, $rs2, $rd"),
797	                 [(set i32:$rd, (OpNode i32:$rs1, i32:$rs2))]>;
798	  def ri  : F3_2 <2, Op3Val,
799	                 (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins IntRegs:$rs1, i32imm:$simm13),
800	                 !strconcat(OpcStr, " $rs1, $simm13, $rd"),
801	                 [(set i32:$rd, (OpNode i32:$rs1, simm13:$simm13))]>;
802	}
803	```
804	
805	So when the `defm` directive is used for the `XOR` and `ADD`
806	instructions, as seen below, it creates four instruction objects: `XORrr`,
807	`XORri`, `ADDrr`, and `ADDri`.
808	
809	```text
810	defm XOR   : F3_12<"xor", 0b000011, xor>;
811	defm ADD   : F3_12<"add", 0b000000, add>;
812	```
813	
814	`SparcInstrInfo.td` also includes definitions for condition codes that are
815	referenced by branch instructions.  The following definitions in
816	`SparcInstrInfo.td` indicate the bit location of the SPARC condition code.
817	For example, the 10{sup}`th` bit represents the "greater than" condition for
818	integers, and the 22{sup}`nd` bit represents the "greater than" condition for
819	floats.
820	
821	```text
822	def ICC_NE  : ICC_VAL< 9>;  // Not Equal
823	def ICC_E   : ICC_VAL< 1>;  // Equal
824	def ICC_G   : ICC_VAL<10>;  // Greater
825	...
826	def FCC_U   : FCC_VAL<23>;  // Unordered
827	def FCC_G   : FCC_VAL<22>;  // Greater
828	def FCC_UG  : FCC_VAL<21>;  // Unordered or Greater
829	...
830	```
831	
832	(Note that `Sparc.h` also defines enums that correspond to the same SPARC
833	condition codes.  Care must be taken to ensure the values in `Sparc.h`
834	correspond to the values in `SparcInstrInfo.td`.  I.e., `SPCC::ICC_NE = 9`,
835	`SPCC::FCC_U = 23` and so on.)
836	
837	### Instruction Operand Mapping
838	
839	The code generator backend maps instruction operands to fields in the
840	instruction.  Whenever a bit in the instruction encoding `Inst` is assigned
841	to field without a concrete value, an operand from the `outs` or `ins` list
842	is expected to have a matching name. This operand then populates that undefined
843	field. For example, the Sparc target defines the `XNORrr` instruction as a
844	`F3_1` format instruction having three operands: the output `$rd`, and the
845	inputs `$rs1`, and `$rs2`.
846	
847	```text
848	def XNORrr  : F3_1<2, 0b000111,
849	                   (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins IntRegs:$rs1, IntRegs:$rs2),
850	                   "xnor $rs1, $rs2, $rd",
851	                   [(set i32:$rd, (not (xor i32:$rs1, i32:$rs2)))]>;
852	```
853	
854	The instruction templates in `SparcInstrFormats.td` show the base class for
855	`F3_1` is `InstSP`.
856	
857	```text
858	class InstSP<dag outs, dag ins, string asmstr, list<dag> pattern> : Instruction {
859	  field bits<32> Inst;
860	  let Namespace = "SP";
861	  bits<2> op;
862	  let Inst{31-30} = op;
863	  dag OutOperandList = outs;
864	  dag InOperandList = ins;
865	  let AsmString   = asmstr;
866	  let Pattern = pattern;
867	}
868	```
869	
870	`InstSP` defines the `op` field, and uses it to define bits 30 and 31 of the
871	instruction, but does not assign a value to it.
872	
873	```text
874	class F3<dag outs, dag ins, string asmstr, list<dag> pattern>
875	    : InstSP<outs, ins, asmstr, pattern> {
876	  bits<5> rd;
877	  bits<6> op3;
878	  bits<5> rs1;
879	  let op{1} = 1;   // Op = 2 or 3
880	  let Inst{29-25} = rd;
881	  let Inst{24-19} = op3;
882	  let Inst{18-14} = rs1;
883	}
884	```
885	
886	`F3` defines the `rd`, `op3`, and `rs1` fields, and uses them in the
887	instruction, and again does not assign values.
888	
889	```text
890	class F3_1<bits<2> opVal, bits<6> op3val, dag outs, dag ins,
891	           string asmstr, list<dag> pattern> : F3<outs, ins, asmstr, pattern> {
892	  bits<8> asi = 0; // asi not currently used
893	  bits<5> rs2;
894	  let op         = opVal;
895	  let op3        = op3val;
896	  let Inst{13}   = 0;     // i field = 0
897	  let Inst{12-5} = asi;   // address space identifier
898	  let Inst{4-0}  = rs2;
899	}
900	```
901	
902	`F3_1` assigns a value to `op` and `op3` fields, and defines the `rs2`
903	field.  Therefore, a `F3_1` format instruction will require a definition for
904	`rd`, `rs1`, and `rs2` in order to fully specify the instruction encoding.
905	
906	The `XNORrr` instruction then provides those three operands in its
907	OutOperandList and InOperandList, which bind to the corresponding fields, and
908	thus complete the instruction encoding.
909	
910	For some instructions, a single operand may contain sub-operands. As shown
911	earlier, the instruction `LDrr` uses an input operand of type `MEMrr`. This
912	operand type contains two register sub-operands, defined by the
913	`MIOperandInfo` value to be `(ops IntRegs, IntRegs)`.
914	
915	```text
916	def LDrr : F3_1 <3, 0b000000, (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins (MEMrr $rs1, $rs2):$addr),
917	                 "ld [$addr], $dst",
918	                 [(set i32:$dst, (load ADDRrr:$addr))]>;
919	```
920	
921	As this instruction is also the `F3_1` format, it will expect operands named
922	`rd`, `rs1`, and `rs2` as well. In order to allow this, a complex operand
923	can optionally give names to each of its sub-operands. In this example
924	`MEMrr`'s first sub-operand is named `$rs1`, the second `$rs2`, and the
925	operand as a whole is also given the name `$addr`.
926	
927	When a particular instruction doesn't use all the operands that the instruction
928	format defines, a constant value may instead be bound to one or all. For
929	example, the `RDASR` instruction only takes a single register operand, so we
930	assign a constant zero to `rs2`:
931	
932	```text
933	let rs2 = 0 in
934	  def RDASR : F3_1<2, 0b101000,
935	                   (outs IntRegs:$rd), (ins ASRRegs:$rs1),
936	                   "rd $rs1, $rd", []>;
937	```
938	
939	#### Instruction Operand Name Mapping
940	
941	TableGen will also generate a function called getNamedOperandIdx() which
942	can be used to look up an operand's index in a MachineInstr based on its
943	TableGen name.  Setting the UseNamedOperandTable bit in an instruction's
944	TableGen definition will add all of its operands to an enumeration
945	llvm::XXX:OpName and also add an entry for it into the OperandMap
946	table, which can be queried using getNamedOperandIdx()
947	
948	```text
949	int DstIndex = SP::getNamedOperandIdx(SP::XNORrr, SP::OpName::dst); // => 0
950	int BIndex = SP::getNamedOperandIdx(SP::XNORrr, SP::OpName::b);     // => 1
951	int CIndex = SP::getNamedOperandIdx(SP::XNORrr, SP::OpName::c);     // => 2
952	int DIndex = SP::getNamedOperandIdx(SP::XNORrr, SP::OpName::d);     // => -1
953	
954	...
955	```
956	
957	The entries in the OpName enum are taken verbatim from the TableGen definitions,
958	so operands with lowercase names will have lower case entries in the enum.
959	
960	To include the getNamedOperandIdx() function in your backend, you will need
961	to define a few preprocessor macros in XXXInstrInfo.cpp and XXXInstrInfo.h.
962	For example:
963	
964	XXXInstrInfo.cpp:
965	
966	```c++
967	// For getNamedOperandIdx() function definition.
968	#define GET_INSTRINFO_NAMED_OPS
969	#include "XXXGenInstrInfo.inc"
970	```
971	
972	XXXInstrInfo.h:
973	
974	```c++
975	// For OpName enum and getNamedOperandIdx declaration.
976	#define GET_INSTRINFO_OPERAND_ENUM
977	#include "XXXGenInstrInfo.inc"
978	```
979	
980	#### Instruction Operand Types
981	
982	TableGen will also generate an enumeration consisting of all named Operand
983	types defined in the backend, in the llvm::XXX::OpTypes namespace.
984	Some common immediate Operand types (for instance i8, i32, i64, f32, f64)
985	are defined for all targets in `include/llvm/Target/Target.td`, and are
986	available in each Target's OpTypes enum.  Also, only named Operand types appear
987	in the enumeration: anonymous types are ignored.
988	For example, the X86 backend defines `brtarget` and `brtarget8`, both
989	instances of the TableGen `Operand` class, which represent branch target
990	operands:
991	
992	```text
993	def brtarget : Operand<OtherVT>;
994	def brtarget8 : Operand<OtherVT>;
995	```
996	
997	This results in:
998	
999	```c++
1000	namespace X86 {
1001	namespace OpTypes {
1002	enum OperandType {
1003	  ...
1004	  brtarget,
1005	  brtarget8,
1006	  ...
1007	  i32imm,
1008	  i64imm,
1009	  ...
1010	  OPERAND_TYPE_LIST_END
1011	} // End namespace OpTypes
1012	} // End namespace X86
1013	```
1014	
1015	In typical TableGen fashion, to use the enum, you will need to define a
1016	preprocessor macro:
1017	
1018	```c++
1019	#define GET_INSTRINFO_OPERAND_TYPES_ENUM // For OpTypes enum
1020	#include "XXXGenInstrInfo.inc"
1021	```

1024	### Instruction Scheduling
1025	
1026	Instruction itineraries can be queried using MCDesc::getSchedClass(). The
1027	value can be named by an enumeration in llvm::XXX::Sched namespace generated
1028	by TableGen in XXXGenInstrInfo.inc. The name of the schedule classes are
1029	the same as provided in XXXSchedule.td plus a default NoItinerary class.
1030	
1031	The schedule models are generated by TableGen by the SubtargetEmitter,
1032	using the `CodeGenSchedModels` class. This is distinct from the itinerary
1033	method of specifying machine resource use.  The tool `utils/schedcover.py`
1034	can be used to determine which instructions have been covered by the
1035	schedule model description and which haven't. The first step is to use the
1036	instructions below to create an output file. Then run `schedcover.py` on the
1037	output file:
1038	
1039	```console
1040	$ <src>/utils/schedcover.py <build>/lib/Target/AArch64/tblGenSubtarget.with
1041	instruction, default, CortexA53Model, CortexA57Model, CycloneModel, ExynosM3Model, FalkorModel, KryoModel, ThunderX2T99Model, ThunderXT8XModel
1042	ABSv16i8, WriteV, , , CyWriteV3, M3WriteNMISC1, FalkorWr_2VXVY_2cyc, KryoWrite_2cyc_XY_XY_150ln, ,
1043	ABSv1i64, WriteV, , , CyWriteV3, M3WriteNMISC1, FalkorWr_1VXVY_2cyc, KryoWrite_2cyc_XY_noRSV_67ln, ,
1044	...
1045	```
1046	
1047	To capture the debug output from generating a schedule model, change to the
1048	appropriate target directory and use the following command:
1049	command with the `subtarget-emitter` debug option:
1050	
1051	```console
1052	$ <build>/bin/llvm-tblgen -debug-only=subtarget-emitter -gen-subtarget \
1053	  -I <src>/lib/Target/<target> -I <src>/include \
1054	  -I <src>/lib/Target <src>/lib/Target/<target>/<target>.td \
1055	  -o <build>/lib/Target/<target>/<target>GenSubtargetInfo.inc.tmp \
1056	  > tblGenSubtarget.dbg 2>&1
1057	```
1058	
1059	Where `<build>` is the build directory, `src` is the source directory,
1060	and `<target>` is the name of the target.
1061	To double check that the above command is what is needed, one can capture the
1062	exact TableGen command from a build by using:
1063	
1064	```console
1065	$ VERBOSE=1 make ...
1066	```
1067	
1068	and search for `llvm-tblgen` commands in the output.

1070	
1071	### Instruction Relation Mapping
1072	
1073	This TableGen feature is used to relate instructions with each other.  It is
1074	particularly useful when you have multiple instruction formats and need to
1075	switch between them after instruction selection.  This entire feature is driven
1076	by relation models which can be defined in `XXXInstrInfo.td` files
1077	according to the target-specific instruction set.  Relation models are defined
1078	using `InstrMapping` class as a base.  TableGen parses all the models
1079	and generates instruction relation maps using the specified information.
1080	Relation maps are emitted as tables in the `XXXGenInstrInfo.inc` file
1081	along with the functions to query them.  For the detailed information on how to
1082	use this feature, please refer to {doc}`HowToUseInstrMappings`.
1083	
1084	### Implement a subclass of `TargetInstrInfo`
1085	
1086	The final step is to hand code portions of `XXXInstrInfo`, which implements
1087	the interface described in `TargetInstrInfo.h` (see {ref}`TargetInstrInfo`).
1088	These functions return `0` or a Boolean or they assert, unless overridden.
1089	Here's a list of functions that are overridden for the SPARC implementation in
1090	`SparcInstrInfo.cpp`:
1091	
1092	* `isLoadFromStackSlot` --- If the specified machine instruction is a direct
1093	  load from a stack slot, return the register number of the destination and the
1094	  `FrameIndex` of the stack slot.
1095	
1096	* `isStoreToStackSlot` --- If the specified machine instruction is a direct
1097	  store to a stack slot, return the register number of the destination and the
1098	  `FrameIndex` of the stack slot.
1099	
1100	* `copyPhysReg` --- Copy values between a pair of physical registers.
1101	
1102	* `storeRegToStackSlot` --- Store a register value to a stack slot.
1103	
1104	* `loadRegFromStackSlot` --- Load a register value from a stack slot.
1105	
1106	* `storeRegToAddr` --- Store a register value to memory.
1107	
1108	* `loadRegFromAddr` --- Load a register value from memory.
1109	
1110	* `foldMemoryOperand` --- Attempt to combine instructions of any load or
1111	  store instruction for the specified operand(s).
1112	
1113	### Branch Folding and If Conversion
1114	
1115	Performance can be improved by combining instructions or by eliminating
1116	instructions that are never reached.  The `analyzeBranch` method in
1117	`XXXInstrInfo` may be implemented to examine conditional instructions and
1118	remove unnecessary instructions.  `analyzeBranch` looks at the end of a
1119	machine basic block (MBB) for opportunities for improvement, such as branch
1120	folding and if conversion.  The `BranchFolder` and `IfConverter` machine
1121	function passes (see the source files `BranchFolding.cpp` and
1122	`IfConversion.cpp` in the `lib/CodeGen` directory) call `analyzeBranch`
1123	to improve the control flow graph that represents the instructions.
1124	
1125	Several implementations of `analyzeBranch` (for ARM, Alpha, and X86) can be
1126	examined as models for your own `analyzeBranch` implementation.  Since SPARC
1127	does not implement a useful `analyzeBranch`, the ARM target implementation is
1128	shown below.
1129	
1130	`analyzeBranch` returns a Boolean value and takes four parameters:
1131	
1132	* `MachineBasicBlock &MBB` --- The incoming block to be examined.
1133	
1134	* `MachineBasicBlock *&TBB` --- A destination block that is returned.  For a
1135	  conditional branch that evaluates to true, `TBB` is the destination.
1136	
1137	* `MachineBasicBlock *&FBB` --- For a conditional branch that evaluates to
1138	  false, `FBB` is returned as the destination.
1139	
1140	* `std::vector<MachineOperand> &Cond` --- List of operands to evaluate a
1141	  condition for a conditional branch.
1142	
1143	In the simplest case, if a block ends without a branch, then it falls through
1144	to the successor block.  No destination blocks are specified for either `TBB`
1145	or `FBB`, so both parameters return `NULL`.  The start of the
1146	`analyzeBranch` (see code below for the ARM target) shows the function
1147	parameters and the code for the simplest case.
1148	
1149	```c++
1150	bool ARMInstrInfo::analyzeBranch(MachineBasicBlock &MBB,
1151	                                 MachineBasicBlock *&TBB,
1152	                                 MachineBasicBlock *&FBB,
1153	                                 std::vector<MachineOperand> &Cond) const
1154	{
1155	  MachineBasicBlock::iterator I = MBB.end();
1156	  if (I == MBB.begin() || !isUnpredicatedTerminator(--I))
1157	    return false;
1158	```
1159	
1160	If a block ends with a single unconditional branch instruction, then
1161	`analyzeBranch` (shown below) should return the destination of that branch in
1162	the `TBB` parameter.
1163	
1164	```c++
1165	  if (LastOpc == ARM::B || LastOpc == ARM::tB) {
1166	    TBB = LastInst->getOperand(0).getMBB();
1167	    return false;
1168	  }
1169	```
1170	
1171	If a block ends with two unconditional branches, then the second branch is
1172	never reached.  In that situation, as shown below, remove the last branch
1173	instruction and return the penultimate branch in the `TBB` parameter.
1174	
1175	```c++
1176	  if ((SecondLastOpc == ARM::B || SecondLastOpc == ARM::tB) &&
1177	      (LastOpc == ARM::B || LastOpc == ARM::tB)) {
1178	    TBB = SecondLastInst->getOperand(0).getMBB();
1179	    I = LastInst;
1180	    I->eraseFromParent();
1181	    return false;
1182	  }
1183	```
1184	
1185	A block may end with a single conditional branch instruction that falls through
1186	to successor block if the condition evaluates to false.  In that case,
1187	`analyzeBranch` (shown below) should return the destination of that
1188	conditional branch in the `TBB` parameter and a list of operands in the
1189	`Cond` parameter to evaluate the condition.
1190	
1191	```c++
1192	  if (LastOpc == ARM::Bcc || LastOpc == ARM::tBcc) {
1193	    // Block ends with fall-through condbranch.
1194	    TBB = LastInst->getOperand(0).getMBB();
1195	    Cond.push_back(LastInst->getOperand(1));
1196	    Cond.push_back(LastInst->getOperand(2));
1197	    return false;
1198	  }
1199	```
1200	
1201	If a block ends with both a conditional branch and an ensuing unconditional
1202	branch, then `analyzeBranch` (shown below) should return the conditional
1203	branch destination (assuming it corresponds to a conditional evaluation of
1204	"`true`") in the `TBB` parameter and the unconditional branch destination
1205	in the `FBB` (corresponding to a conditional evaluation of "`false`").  A
1206	list of operands to evaluate the condition should be returned in the `Cond`
1207	parameter.
1208	
1209	```c++
1210	  unsigned SecondLastOpc = SecondLastInst->getOpcode();
1211	
1212	  if ((SecondLastOpc == ARM::Bcc && LastOpc == ARM::B) ||
1213	      (SecondLastOpc == ARM::tBcc && LastOpc == ARM::tB)) {
1214	    TBB =  SecondLastInst->getOperand(0).getMBB();
1215	    Cond.push_back(SecondLastInst->getOperand(1));
1216	    Cond.push_back(SecondLastInst->getOperand(2));
1217	    FBB = LastInst->getOperand(0).getMBB();
1218	    return false;
1219	  }
1220	```
1221	
1222	For the last two cases (ending with a single conditional branch or ending with
1223	one conditional and one unconditional branch), the operands returned in the
1224	`Cond` parameter can be passed to methods of other instructions to create new
1225	branches or perform other operations.  An implementation of `analyzeBranch`
1226	requires the helper methods `removeBranch` and `insertBranch` to manage
1227	subsequent operations.
1228	
1229	`analyzeBranch` should return false indicating success in most circumstances.
1230	`analyzeBranch` should only return true when the method is stumped about what
1231	to do, for example, if a block has three terminating branches.
1232	`analyzeBranch` may return true if it encounters a terminator it cannot
1233	handle, such as an indirect branch.
1234	
1235	(instruction-selector)=
1236	
1237	## Instruction Selector
1238	
1239	LLVM uses a `SelectionDAG` to represent LLVM IR instructions, and nodes of
1240	the `SelectionDAG` ideally represent native target instructions.  During code
1241	generation, instruction selection passes are performed to convert non-native
1242	DAG instructions into native target-specific instructions.  The pass described
1243	in `XXXISelDAGToDAG.cpp` is used to match patterns and perform DAG-to-DAG
1244	instruction selection.  Optionally, a pass may be defined (in
1245	`XXXBranchSelector.cpp`) to perform similar DAG-to-DAG operations for branch
1246	instructions.  Later, the code in `XXXISelLowering.cpp` replaces or removes
1247	operations and data types not supported natively (legalizes) in a
1248	`SelectionDAG`.
1249	
1250	TableGen generates code for instruction selection using the following target
1251	description input files:
1252	
1253	* `XXXInstrInfo.td` --- Contains definitions of instructions in a
1254	  target-specific instruction set, generates `XXXGenDAGISel.inc`, which is
1255	  included in `XXXISelDAGToDAG.cpp`.
1256	
1257	* `XXXCallingConv.td` --- Contains the calling and return value conventions
1258	  for the target architecture, and it generates `XXXGenCallingConv.inc`,
1259	  which is included in `XXXISelLowering.cpp`.
1260	
1261	The implementation of an instruction selection pass must include a header that
1262	declares the `FunctionPass` class or a subclass of `FunctionPass`.  In
1263	`XXXTargetMachine.cpp`, a Pass Manager (PM) should add each instruction
1264	selection pass into the queue of passes to run.
1265	
1266	The LLVM static compiler (`llc`) is an excellent tool for visualizing the
1267	contents of DAGs.  To display the `SelectionDAG` before or after specific
1268	processing phases, use the command line options for `llc`, described at
1269	{ref}`SelectionDAG-Process`.
1270	
1271	To describe instruction selector behavior, you should add patterns for lowering
1272	LLVM code into a `SelectionDAG` as the last parameter of the instruction
1273	definitions in `XXXInstrInfo.td`.  For example, in `SparcInstrInfo.td`,
1274	this entry defines a register store operation, and the last parameter describes
1275	a pattern with the store DAG operator.
1276	
1277	```text
1278	def STrr  : F3_1< 3, 0b000100, (outs), (ins MEMrr:$addr, IntRegs:$src),
1279	                 "st $src, [$addr]", [(store i32:$src, ADDRrr:$addr)]>;
1280	```
1281	
1282	`ADDRrr` is a memory mode that is also defined in `SparcInstrInfo.td`:
1283	
1284	```text
1285	def ADDRrr : ComplexPattern<i32, 2, "SelectADDRrr", [], []>;
1286	```
1287	
1288	The definition of `ADDRrr` refers to `SelectADDRrr`, which is a function
1289	defined in an implementation of the Instructor Selector (such as
1290	`SparcISelDAGToDAG.cpp`).
1291	
1292	In `lib/Target/TargetSelectionDAG.td`, the DAG operator for store is defined
1293	below:
1294	
1295	```text
1296	def store : PatFrag<(ops node:$val, node:$ptr),
1297	                    (unindexedstore node:$val, node:$ptr)> {
1298	  let IsStore = true;
1299	  let IsTruncStore = false;
1300	}
1301	```
1302	
1303	`XXXInstrInfo.td` also generates (in `XXXGenDAGISel.inc`) the
1304	`SelectCode` method that is used to call the appropriate processing method
1305	for an instruction.  In this example, `SelectCode` calls `Select_ISD_STORE`
1306	for the `ISD::STORE` opcode.
1307	
1308	```c++
1309	SDNode *SelectCode(SDValue N) {
1310	  ...
1311	  MVT::ValueType NVT = N.getNode()->getValueType(0);
1312	  switch (N.getOpcode()) {
1313	  case ISD::STORE: {
1314	    switch (NVT) {
1315	    default:
1316	      return Select_ISD_STORE(N);
1317	      break;
1318	    }
1319	    break;
1320	  }
1321	  ...
1322	```
1323	
1324	The pattern for `STrr` is matched, so elsewhere in `XXXGenDAGISel.inc`,
1325	code for `STrr` is created for `Select_ISD_STORE`.  The `Emit_22` method
1326	is also generated in `XXXGenDAGISel.inc` to complete the processing of this
1327	instruction.
1328	
1329	```c++
1330	SDNode *Select_ISD_STORE(const SDValue &N) {
1331	  SDValue Chain = N.getOperand(0);
1332	  if (Predicate_store(N.getNode())) {
1333	    SDValue N1 = N.getOperand(1);
1334	    SDValue N2 = N.getOperand(2);
1335	    SDValue CPTmp0;
1336	    SDValue CPTmp1;
1337	
1338	    // Pattern: (st:void i32:i32:$src,
1339	    //           ADDRrr:i32:$addr)<<P:Predicate_store>>
1340	    // Emits: (STrr:void ADDRrr:i32:$addr, IntRegs:i32:$src)
1341	    // Pattern complexity = 13  cost = 1  size = 0
1342	    if (SelectADDRrr(N, N2, CPTmp0, CPTmp1) &&
1343	        N1.getNode()->getValueType(0) == MVT::i32 &&
1344	        N2.getNode()->getValueType(0) == MVT::i32) {
1345	      return Emit_22(N, SP::STrr, CPTmp0, CPTmp1);
1346	    }
1347	...
1348	```
1349	
1350	### The SelectionDAG Legalize Phase
1351	
1352	The Legalize phase converts a DAG to use types and operations that are natively
1353	supported by the target.  For natively unsupported types and operations, you
1354	need to add code to the target-specific `XXXTargetLowering` implementation to
1355	convert unsupported types and operations to supported ones.
1356	
1357	In the constructor for the `XXXTargetLowering` class, first use the
1358	`addRegisterClass` method to specify which types are supported and which
1359	register classes are associated with them.  The code for the register classes
1360	are generated by TableGen from `XXXRegisterInfo.td` and placed in
1361	`XXXGenRegisterInfo.h.inc`.  For example, the implementation of the
1362	constructor for the SparcTargetLowering class (in `SparcISelLowering.cpp`)
1363	starts with the following code:
1364	
1365	```c++
1366	addRegisterClass(MVT::i32, SP::IntRegsRegisterClass);
1367	addRegisterClass(MVT::f32, SP::FPRegsRegisterClass);
1368	addRegisterClass(MVT::f64, SP::DFPRegsRegisterClass);
1369	```
1370	
1371	You should examine the node types in the `ISD` namespace
1372	(`include/llvm/CodeGen/SelectionDAGNodes.h`) and determine which operations
1373	the target natively supports.  For operations that do **not** have native
1374	support, add a callback to the constructor for the `XXXTargetLowering` class,
1375	so the instruction selection process knows what to do.  The `TargetLowering`
1376	class callback methods (declared in `llvm/Target/TargetLowering.h`) are:
1377	
1378	* `setOperationAction` --- General operation.
1379	* `setLoadExtAction` --- Load with extension.
1380	* `setTruncStoreAction` --- Truncating store.
1381	* `setIndexedLoadAction` --- Indexed load.
1382	* `setIndexedStoreAction` --- Indexed store.
1383	* `setConvertAction` --- Type conversion.
1384	* `setCondCodeAction` --- Support for a given condition code.
1385	
1386	Note: on older releases, `setLoadXAction` is used instead of
1387	`setLoadExtAction`.  Also, on older releases, `setCondCodeAction` may not
1388	be supported.  Examine your release to see what methods are specifically
1389	supported.
1390	
1391	These callbacks are used to determine that an operation does or does not work
1392	with a specified type (or types).  And in all cases, the third parameter is a
1393	`LegalAction` type enum value: `Promote`, `Expand`, `Custom`, or
1394	`Legal`.  `SparcISelLowering.cpp` contains examples of all four
1395	`LegalAction` values.
1396	
1397	#### Promote
1398	
1399	For an operation without native support for a given type, the specified type
1400	may be promoted to a larger type that is supported.  For example, SPARC does
1401	not support a sign-extending load for Boolean values (`i1` type), so in
1402	`SparcISelLowering.cpp` the third parameter below, `Promote`, changes
1403	`i1` type values to a large type before loading.
1404	
1405	```c++
1406	setLoadExtAction(ISD::SEXTLOAD, MVT::i1, Promote);
1407	```
1408	
1409	#### Expand
1410	
1411	For a type without native support, a value may need to be broken down further,
1412	rather than promoted.  For an operation without native support, a combination
1413	of other operations may be used to similar effect.  In SPARC, the
1414	floating-point sine and cosine trig operations are supported by expansion to
1415	other operations, as indicated by the third parameter, `Expand`, to
1416	`setOperationAction`:
1417	
1418	```c++
1419	setOperationAction(ISD::FSIN, MVT::f32, Expand);
1420	setOperationAction(ISD::FCOS, MVT::f32, Expand);
1421	```
1422	
1423	#### Custom
1424	
1425	For some operations, simple type promotion or operation expansion may be
1426	insufficient.  In some cases, a special intrinsic function must be implemented.
1427	
1428	For example, a constant value may require special treatment, or an operation
1429	may require spilling and restoring registers in the stack and working with
1430	register allocators.
1431	
1432	As seen in `SparcISelLowering.cpp` code below, to perform a type conversion
1433	from a floating point value to a signed integer, first the
1434	`setOperationAction` should be called with `Custom` as the third parameter:
1435	
1436	```c++
1437	setOperationAction(ISD::FP_TO_SINT, MVT::i32, Custom);
1438	```
1439	
1440	In the `LowerOperation` method, for each `Custom` operation, a case
1441	statement should be added to indicate what function to call.  In the following
1442	code, an `FP_TO_SINT` opcode will call the `LowerFP_TO_SINT` method:
1443	
1444	```c++
1445	SDValue SparcTargetLowering::LowerOperation(SDValue Op, SelectionDAG &DAG) {
1446	  switch (Op.getOpcode()) {
1447	  case ISD::FP_TO_SINT: return LowerFP_TO_SINT(Op, DAG);
1448	  ...
1449	  }
1450	}
1451	```
1452	
1453	Finally, the `LowerFP_TO_SINT` method is implemented, using an FP register to
1454	convert the floating-point value to an integer.
1455	
1456	```c++
1457	static SDValue LowerFP_TO_SINT(SDValue Op, SelectionDAG &DAG) {
1458	  assert(Op.getValueType() == MVT::i32);
1459	  Op = DAG.getNode(SPISD::FTOI, MVT::f32, Op.getOperand(0));
1460	  return DAG.getNode(ISD::BITCAST, MVT::i32, Op);
1461	}
1462	```
1463	
1464	#### Legal
1465	
1466	The `Legal` `LegalizeAction` enum value simply indicates that an operation
1467	**is** natively supported.  `Legal` represents the default condition, so it
1468	is rarely used.  In `SparcISelLowering.cpp`, the action for `CTPOP` (an
1469	operation to count the bits set in an integer) is natively supported only for
1470	SPARC v9.  The following code enables the `Expand` conversion technique for
1471	non-v9 SPARC implementations.
1472	
1473	```c++
1474	setOperationAction(ISD::CTPOP, MVT::i32, Expand);
1475	...
1476	if (TM.getSubtarget<SparcSubtarget>().isV9())
1477	  setOperationAction(ISD::CTPOP, MVT::i32, Legal);
1478	```

1482	### Calling Conventions
1483	
1484	To support target-specific calling conventions, `XXXGenCallingConv.td` uses
1485	interfaces (such as `CCIfType` and `CCAssignToReg`) that are defined in
1486	`lib/Target/TargetCallingConv.td`.  TableGen can take the target descriptor
1487	file `XXXGenCallingConv.td` and generate the header file
1488	`XXXGenCallingConv.inc`, which is typically included in
1489	`XXXISelLowering.cpp`.  You can use the interfaces in
1490	`TargetCallingConv.td` to specify:
1491	
1492	* The order of parameter allocation.
1493	
1494	* Where parameters and return values are placed (that is, on the stack or in
1495	  registers).
1496	
1497	* Which registers may be used.
1498	
1499	* Whether the caller or callee unwinds the stack.
1500	
1501	The following example demonstrates the use of the `CCIfType` and
1502	`CCAssignToReg` interfaces.  If the `CCIfType` predicate is true (that is,
1503	if the current argument is of type `f32` or `f64`), then the action is
1504	performed.  In this case, the `CCAssignToReg` action assigns the argument
1505	value to the first available register: either `R0` or `R1`.
1506	
1507	```text
1508	CCIfType<[f32,f64], CCAssignToReg<[R0, R1]>>
1509	```
1510	
1511	`SparcCallingConv.td` contains definitions for a target-specific return-value
1512	calling convention (`RetCC_Sparc32`) and a basic 32-bit C calling convention
1513	(`CC_Sparc32`).  The definition of `RetCC_Sparc32` (shown below) indicates
1514	which registers are used for specified scalar return types.  A single-precision
1515	float is returned to register `F0`, and a double-precision float goes to
1516	register `D0`.  A 32-bit integer is returned in register `I0` or `I1`.
1517	
1518	```text
1519	def RetCC_Sparc32 : CallingConv<[
1520	  CCIfType<[i32], CCAssignToReg<[I0, I1]>>,
1521	  CCIfType<[f32], CCAssignToReg<[F0]>>,
1522	  CCIfType<[f64], CCAssignToReg<[D0]>>
1523	]>;
1524	```
1525	
1526	The definition of `CC_Sparc32` in `SparcCallingConv.td` introduces
1527	`CCAssignToStack`, which assigns the value to a stack slot with the specified
1528	size and alignment.  In the example below, the first parameter, 4, indicates
1529	the size of the slot, and the second parameter, also 4, indicates the stack
1530	alignment along 4-byte units.  (Special cases: if size is zero, then the ABI
1531	size is used; if alignment is zero, then the ABI alignment is used.)
1532	
1533	```text
1534	def CC_Sparc32 : CallingConv<[
1535	  // All arguments get passed in integer registers if there is space.
1536	  CCIfType<[i32, f32, f64], CCAssignToReg<[I0, I1, I2, I3, I4, I5]>>,
1537	  CCAssignToStack<4, 4>
1538	]>;
1539	```
1540	
1541	`CCDelegateTo` is another commonly used interface, which tries to find a
1542	specified sub-calling convention, and, if a match is found, it is invoked.  In
1543	the following example (in `X86CallingConv.td`), the definition of
1544	`RetCC_X86_32_C` ends with `CCDelegateTo`.  After the current value is
1545	assigned to the register `ST0` or `ST1`, the `RetCC_X86Common` is
1546	invoked.
1547	
1548	```text
1549	def RetCC_X86_32_C : CallingConv<[
1550	  CCIfType<[f32], CCAssignToReg<[ST0, ST1]>>,
1551	  CCIfType<[f64], CCAssignToReg<[ST0, ST1]>>,
1552	  CCDelegateTo<RetCC_X86Common>
1553	]>;
1554	```
1555	
1556	`CCIfCC` is an interface that attempts to match the given name to the current
1557	calling convention.  If the name identifies the current calling convention,
1558	then a specified action is invoked.  In the following example (in
1559	`X86CallingConv.td`), if the `Fast` calling convention is in use, then
1560	`RetCC_X86_32_Fast` is invoked.  If the `SSECall` calling convention is in
1561	use, then `RetCC_X86_32_SSE` is invoked.
1562	
1563	```text
1564	def RetCC_X86_32 : CallingConv<[
1565	  CCIfCC<"CallingConv::Fast", CCDelegateTo<RetCC_X86_32_Fast>>,
1566	  CCIfCC<"CallingConv::X86_SSECall", CCDelegateTo<RetCC_X86_32_SSE>>,
1567	  CCDelegateTo<RetCC_X86_32_C>
1568	]>;
1569	```
1570	
1571	`CCAssignToRegAndStack` is the same as `CCAssignToReg`, but also allocates
1572	a stack slot, when some register is used. Basically, it works like:
1573	`CCIf<CCAssignToReg<regList>, CCAssignToStack<size, align>>`.
1574	
1575	```text
1576	class CCAssignToRegAndStack<list<Register> regList, int size, int align>
1577	    : CCAssignToReg<regList> {
1578	  int Size = size;
1579	  int Align = align;
1580	}
1581	```
1582	
1583	Other calling convention interfaces include:
1584	
1585	* `CCIf <predicate, action>` --- If the predicate matches, apply the action.
1586	
1587	* `CCIfInReg <action>` --- If the argument is marked with the "`inreg`"
1588	  attribute, then apply the action.
1589	
1590	* `CCIfNest <action>` --- If the argument is marked with the "`nest`"
1591	  attribute, then apply the action.
1592	
1593	* `CCIfNotVarArg <action>` --- If the current function does not take a
1594	  variable number of arguments, apply the action.
1595	
1596	* `CCAssignToRegWithShadow <registerList, shadowList>` --- similar to
1597	  `CCAssignToReg`, but with a shadow list of registers.
1598	
1599	* `CCPassByVal <size, align>` --- Assign value to a stack slot with the
1600	  minimum specified size and alignment.
1601	
1602	* `CCPromoteToType <type>` --- Promote the current value to the specified
1603	  type.
1604	
1605	* `CallingConv <[actions]>` --- Define each calling convention that is
1606	  supported.

1608	## Assembly Printer
1609	
1610	During the code emission stage, the code generator may utilize an LLVM pass to
1611	produce assembly output.  To do this, you want to implement the code for a
1612	printer that converts LLVM IR to a GAS-format assembly language for your target
1613	machine, using the following steps:
1614	
1615	* Define all the assembly strings for your target, adding them to the
1616	  instructions defined in the `XXXInstrInfo.td` file.  (See
1617	  {ref}`instruction-set`.)  TableGen will produce an output file
1618	  (`XXXGenAsmWriter.inc`) with an implementation of the `printInstruction`
1619	  method for the `XXXAsmPrinter` class.
1620	
1621	* Write `XXXTargetAsmInfo.h`, which contains the bare-bones declaration of
1622	  the `XXXTargetAsmInfo` class (a subclass of `TargetAsmInfo`).
1623	
1624	* Write `XXXTargetAsmInfo.cpp`, which contains target-specific values for
1625	  `TargetAsmInfo` properties and sometimes new implementations for methods.
1626	
1627	* Write `XXXAsmPrinter.cpp`, which implements the `AsmPrinter` class that
1628	  performs the LLVM-to-assembly conversion.
1629	
1630	The code in `XXXTargetAsmInfo.h` is usually a trivial declaration of the
1631	`XXXTargetAsmInfo` class for use in `XXXTargetAsmInfo.cpp`.  Similarly,
1632	`XXXTargetAsmInfo.cpp` usually has a few declarations of `XXXTargetAsmInfo`
1633	replacement values that override the default values in `TargetAsmInfo.cpp`.
1634	For example in `SparcTargetAsmInfo.cpp`:
1635	
1636	```c++
1637	SparcTargetAsmInfo::SparcTargetAsmInfo(const SparcTargetMachine &TM) {
1638	  Data16bitsDirective = "\t.half\t";
1639	  Data32bitsDirective = "\t.word\t";
1640	  Data64bitsDirective = 0;  // .xword is only supported by V9.
1641	  ZeroDirective = "\t.skip\t";
1642	  CommentString = "!";
1643	  ConstantPoolSection = "\t.section \".rodata\",#alloc\n";
1644	}
1645	```
1646	
1647	The X86 assembly printer implementation (`X86TargetAsmInfo`) is an example
1648	where the target-specific `TargetAsmInfo` class uses an overridden methods:
1649	`ExpandInlineAsm`.
1650	
1651	A target-specific implementation of `AsmPrinter` is written in
1652	`XXXAsmPrinter.cpp`, which implements the `AsmPrinter` class that converts
1653	the LLVM to printable assembly.  The implementation must include the following
1654	headers that have declarations for the `AsmPrinter` and
1655	`MachineFunctionPass` classes.  The `MachineFunctionPass` is a subclass of
1656	`FunctionPass`.
1657	
1658	```c++
1659	#include "llvm/CodeGen/AsmPrinter.h"
1660	#include "llvm/CodeGen/MachineFunctionPass.h"
1661	```
1662	
1663	As a `FunctionPass`, `AsmPrinter` first calls `doInitialization` to set
1664	up the `AsmPrinter`.  In `SparcAsmPrinter`, a `Mangler` object is
1665	instantiated to process variable names.
1666	
1667	In `XXXAsmPrinter.cpp`, the `runOnMachineFunction` method (declared in
1668	`MachineFunctionPass`) must be implemented for `XXXAsmPrinter`.  In
1669	`MachineFunctionPass`, the `runOnFunction` method invokes
1670	`runOnMachineFunction`.  Target-specific implementations of
1671	`runOnMachineFunction` differ, but generally do the following to process each
1672	machine function:
1673	
1674	* Call `SetupMachineFunction` to perform initialization.
1675	
1676	* Call `EmitConstantPool` to print out (to the output stream) constants which
1677	  have been spilled to memory.
1678	
1679	* Call `EmitJumpTableInfo` to print out jump tables used by the current
1680	  function.
1681	
1682	* Print out the label for the current function.
1683	
1684	* Print out the code for the function, including basic block labels and the
1685	  assembly for the instruction (using `printInstruction`)
1686	
1687	The `XXXAsmPrinter` implementation must also include the code generated by
1688	TableGen that is output in the `XXXGenAsmWriter.inc` file.  The code in
1689	`XXXGenAsmWriter.inc` contains an implementation of the `printInstruction`
1690	method that may call these methods:
1691	
1692	* `printOperand`
1693	* `printMemOperand`
1694	* `printCCOperand` (for conditional statements)
1695	* `printDataDirective`
1696	* `printDeclare`
1697	* `printImplicitDef`
1698	* `printInlineAsm`
1699	
1700	The implementations of `printDeclare`, `printImplicitDef`,
1701	`printInlineAsm`, and `printLabel` in `AsmPrinter.cpp` are generally
1702	adequate for printing assembly and do not need to be overridden.
1703	
1704	The `printOperand` method is implemented with a long `switch`/`case`
1705	statement for the type of operand: register, immediate, basic block, external
1706	symbol, global address, constant pool index, or jump table index.  For an
1707	instruction with a memory address operand, the `printMemOperand` method
1708	should be implemented to generate the proper output.  Similarly,
1709	`printCCOperand` should be used to print a conditional operand.
1710	
1711	`doFinalization` should be overridden in `XXXAsmPrinter`, and it should be
1712	called to shut down the assembly printer.  During `doFinalization`, global
1713	variables and constants are printed to output.
